entries.title: 3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
entries.summary: Reconstruction has progressed in the three years since the 2023 Morocco earthquake, but some survivors are still living in tents. Locals are divided as to how successful it's been, and whether state aid is enough.
entries.content:
Africa

3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help

September 7, 2026

Reconstruction has progressed in the three years since the 2023 Morocco earthquake, but some survivors are still living in tents. Locals are divided as to how successful it's been, and whether state aid is enough.

On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction.

In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later.

He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it's smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake.

"I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding," he told DW. "I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I'm comfortable in it. I'm at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven't lost any of them."

Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it's a different story. Larbi Ait Jelloulat, also 72, is sitting in front of a pile of rubble that was once his house.

"I want to know where my rights have gone," he said angrily. "Who took what's rightfully mine? For three years, I've been going from one department to another, from one complaint to another, from one petition to another, just looking for an answer. Why have I been excluded? Am I not a Moroccan citizen?"

Ait Jelloulat was formerly a council employee and saved for years in order to build the large home that was destroyed in the 2023 earthquake. As far as he can tell, bureaucratic issues mean he must prove he was a resident in the area.

"My only dream was to spend the rest of my life in my own home, a rest after years of service," he explained. "Now they say I'm not a resident … Where's the logic in that?"

Why such different experiences?

Reconstruction seems to be happening faster in Ighermane, the village where Ait Belaid lives. About 90% of the village is rebuilt and most residents' lives are back to normal, said Omar Saeed from the Ighermane Association for Development and Solidarity.

Of the village's around 150 families, 114 received state support of some kind, although most also had to contribute some of their own money to rebuild.

Meanwhile, in Azgour, where Ait Jelloulat lives, there's been more to do. Azgour was the village most impacted by the earthquake in the area.

There, about 76 families have had help with reconstruction, Ait Jelloulat said, while 56 others are still waiting for help. "What's more, the 76 families who rebuilt their homes in a different location are also having problems connecting to water and electricity," he added.

Rebuilding difficult in remote mountain villages

According to a March statement from the High Atlas Development Agency, or ADHA, which was established in October 2023 to bring help to affected areas, 54,425 homes have been built or rehabilitated and more than 3,000 homes are still under construction. The government has given out more than 7.2 billion dirhams (€656 million/$770 million) to affected families. The sum includes funds to help rebuild as well as monthly emergency aid payments.

In terms of the pace of construction, Marrakech-based architect Mohamed Belmejjad believes the state is actually doing fairly well. "I believe the progress so far, relative to the timeframe, to be positive," he told DW.

Given the circumstances, it would be hard for things to have gone much faster, he suggested.

Immediately after the earthquake, it was difficult to reach affected locations, especially remote mountain villages and towns. Then rubble had to be cleared before building could begin.

After that, other factors complicated reconstruction, including the distance of some villages from paved roads, the difficulty of transporting building materials in and debris out, problems with connecting water and power, and the need to relocate whole villages and construction sites to avoid dangers like landslides. There's also a need to respect local building traditions, ensuring that construction materials are solid and will last.

"We also lack the necessary expertise here, whether that's in terms of architects, design offices, contractors or even the labor required for construction," Belmejjad pointed out. Given all that has happened reconstruction could actually be considered ahead of schedule, he suggested.

'No one has remembered us'

Despite that, the National Coordination for Al Haouz Earthquake Victims reports receiving complaints from more than 3,000 families who haven't had any state help.

Montasser Itri, a member of the organization, explains that some of these families were excluded because they had moved to other parts of the country to work and their national identity cards then show them as residents of places unaffected by the 2023 earthquake.

"The government is trying to make us, the victims of the Al Haouz earthquake, into mere statistics linked to the progress of construction and the removal of tents," Itri told DW, "rather than treating us as human beings and with dignity."

That's why the coordinating committee is already demanding an independent and transparent investigation into how local authorities have handled the payouts. In the past they've organized demonstrations outside parliament buildings in the capital, Rabat, to demand compensation and rehousing solutions and to accuse local authorities of failing to honor commitments.

Other impacted locals are hoping the upcoming general election, slated for September 23, might make a difference.

"[Prime Minister Aziz] Akhannouch promised us a solution to the issue and God knows we are waiting," said Fawzia Aliban, whose home in Amizmiz was damaged in the earthquake. "We hope the problems will be resolved because I was denied benefits even though my house is on the verge of collapse."

"Three years have passed, and no one has remembered us […] but recently some political figures turned up and promised to solve the problem," added Mohamed Belkaid, who is still living in a tent in the Amizmiz area with his four children.

He hasn't received any aid to rebuild because he is listed as a tenant, not an owner, and is not optimistic things will change.

"They promised to review our files, asking us to trust them and to vote for them," he complained. "But this is exploitation. If they truly wanted to solve the problem, they would have done so before the elections. Where have they been all these years?"

This article was originally written in Arabic.

entries.title: Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back
entries.summary: As his latest movie, "Bucking Fastard," premiered at the Venice Film Festival, DW talked to the boundary-breaking director.
entries.content:
Europe

Werner Herzog: Germany's wild man of cinema is back

September 7, 2026

As his latest movie, "Bucking Fastard," premiered at the Venice Film Festival, DW talked to the boundary-breaking director.

When Werner Herzog needed a title for his memoirs, he reached back to one of his own films: "Every Man for Himself and God Against All," the original German title of his 1974 feature known in English as "The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser." For Herzog, perhaps the last wild man of European cinema, it's less a title than a worldview.

Over more than 60 years as a provocative, boundary-breaking filmmaker, Herzog has made films on the slopes of active volcanoes, and in the middle of the Sahara. He's filmed in the jungle and north of the Arctic Circle, telling stories of characters who live at the edges of human achievement. Often, in making these films, Herzog has pushed himself, and his collaborators, to the edge as well.

Now 84, Werner Herzog shows no signs of slowing down. He's back with a new feature film, "Bucking Fastard," his first drama in seven years, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival.

'Bucking Fastard:' two sisters, totally in sync

The film is the story of Jean and Joan Holbrooke, two sisters who speak, think and move in unison. They even share the same dreams and love the same undeserving man.

Hollywood stars and real-life siblings Kate and Rooney Mara play the sisters, their performances synced up to an uncanny degree.

The film is loosely inspired by real-life twin sisters Freda and Greta Chaplin, who became a tabloid sensation in England in the 1980s. The film's title is a reference to an inadvertent simultaneous spoonerism the sisters made in court, when describing their former lover.

In Herzog's version, the Holbrooke sisters, after being rejected by their true love (played by Orlando Bloom), decamp to the wilds of Ireland and begin digging a tunnel in a cave, convinced they can dig their way to the Orkney Islands — a mythical place where true love is possible.

Reaching out for the extraordinary

The Holbrooke sisters are two ecstatic dreamers striving to do the impossible. Typical Herzog protagonists.

Herzog himself sees the through-line.

"With 'Fitzcarraldo,' there is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain," he told DW in Venice.

Herzog was referring to his 1982 epic adventure drama in which he had his crew actually haul a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle to tell the story of a man who dreams of building an opera house in the middle of the rainforest.

Similarly, added the director, "Bucking Fastard" is "the dream of an ideal country, which doesn't really exist."

In the world of Werner Herzog, art imitates life, and vice versa.

While filming "Aguirre, the Wrath of God" (1972), the story of a mad conquistador in search of El Dorado, Herzog and his crew, including star Klaus Kinski, nearly went mad themselves.

In his 1999 documentary on Kinski, "My Best Fiend," Herzog recounts how the actor threatened to leave the film. If he did, the director told him, he would follow him and shoot him dead.

Real people, real extremes

Herzog is, if anything, even better known as a documentarian and his real-life protagonists are as extreme as his fictional characters.

In "Grizzly Man" (2005), he ponders the life of Timothy Treadwell, an animal rights activist who spent years getting up close and personal with bears in the wild, until one of them ate him.

"Little Dieter Needs to Fly" (1997) follows the German-born American Vietnam War pilot Dieter Dengler, who survived a harrowing escape from a Laotian prison camp.

For "La Soufriere" (1977), Herzog filmed in an abandoned town in Guadeloupe, next to a volcano on the brink of eruption, to talk to the one man who refuses to evacuate.

Films as our 'collective dreams'

Herzog sees little difference between his fiction and non-fiction films. He admits to inventing scenes for his documentaries, and to filming real events for his features.

For "Rescue Dawn" (2006), a feature adaptation of the Dieter Dengler story, Herzog got star Christian Bale to devour live maggots on camera (the director showed him how, gobbling up some himself) and wrestle with a real live snake for a scene.

"Film does not have so much to do with reality as it does with our collective dreams," Herzog said.

He thinks of himself less as a director than "as a poet."

'Just go out and do it'

In his often haunting tales of man's struggle with nature, Herzog aims to achieve an "ecstatic truth" beyond mere reality. His goal, he said, is not to depict the extreme as bizarre or extraordinary. It is to inspire everyone to be extraordinary.

"Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range," he told DW. "[The message] is very simple: Just go out and do it."

Rooney Mara agreed: "Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that's not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that."

A divided response in Venice

"Bucking Fastard" is an odd, and oddly funny film, especially for a Herzog movie.

"Thank you for seeing that," said Herzog, who argued there is humor in all his films, if you look for it. "Sometimes it's a dark humor. Sometimes it's a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn't understand. For Americans, it's easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it."

The Venice audience gave "Bucking Fastard" a warm welcome, but critics were more divided. A few embraced Herzog's new piece of ecstatic weirdness. Most dismissed it as confusing, clunky and utterly nonsensical. An "uddled-mup fairytale," wrote one, playing on the film's mixed up title.

Why Herzog still matters

Herzog critics are legion, but his fans probably don't care. The 84-year-old director is as popular as he's ever been. He launched an Instagram account last year, even though he still doesn't own a smartphone, and it has become a huge hit with Gen Z.

"My younger son does it, he knows how, and he tells me 85% of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old," Herzog said. "And because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden [young people] are discovering it."

Mara said Herzog remains an inspiration, as "a singular human being [who] really doesn't give a sh**." Speaking to the German director, she noted: "You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that's what we all want to do."

Next stop: outer space?

For his part, Herzog is not slowing down. He's already put "Bucking Fastard" behind him and is deep in post-production on his new film and has a Taschen photo book in progress.

And he still hasn't given up on his impossible dream: making a film in space.

"I spoke to NASA, but they didn't take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon [but] he refused to take me on board," he said. "[But] Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Nicaragua challenges German arms exports to Israel at ICJ
entries.summary: Germany has asked the International Court of Justice to dismiss the case on jurisdiction grounds. It also said its arms exports to Israel were documented, published, and subject to more stringent checks than most.
entries.content:
Germany

Nicaragua challenges German arms exports to Israel at ICJ

September 7, 2026

Germany has asked the International Court of Justice to dismiss the case on jurisdiction grounds. It also said its arms exports to Israel were documented, published, and subject to more stringent checks than most.

Germany on Monday asked the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to dismiss a case brought by Nicaragua, accusing Berlin of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention by supplying arms to Israel amid its war with Hamas in Gaza. 

If the ICJ, otherwise known as the World Court, decided to hear the case, the process would likely take years and be contingent on the findings from separate Gaza-related cases in The Hague.

But Germany is arguing it shouldn't even go that far, saying that Nicaragua did not follow proper processes and that the dispute does not fall in the international court's jurisdiction.

Nicaragua, on the other hand, argues that the case should be heard because it and Germany are both signatories to the Genocide Convention — despite neither side being directly involved in Israel and Hamas' war in Gaza and although the ICJ hearing on whether Israel committed genocidal acts in Gaza could take years.

What is the case about?

Nicaragua accuses Germany of aiding and abetting genocide in Gaza by selling weapons to Israel, some of which it says have been used in Gaza.

An initial bid for an emergency injunction ordering a halt to exports failed in 2024 at the height of the war in Gaza, but Germany also failed in its bid to have the case summarily and permanently dismissed at the earliest opportunity. 

The German government suspended weapons exports to Israel for around three months in 2025 as the conflict continued and casualty figures rose. But it has since restarted them amid the truce struck late last year that largely stopped the fighting, without ending Israeli strikes entirely.

Germany walks a fine historical and political line in the case.

On the one hand, the 1948 Genocide Convention was born in very large part from the lessons of the Holocaust and the spirit of "never again" after World War II. But to the same token, Germany has always sought to maintain close and cooperative ties with Israel, a state formed in very large part as a consequence of its mass extermination of Jews in Europe. It considers Israeli security part of its own raison d'etre as a modern democratic state.

Israel's war in Gaza was launched against Hamas after Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel. October 7 was the single deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Hamas is a Palestinian Islamist group based in the Gaza Strip.

What is Germany arguing?

Germany is arguing both that the case should be dismissed on procedural grounds, and that Nicaragua's allegation of aiding and abetting genocide is unsubstantiated.

Although Germany, Nicaragua and Israel are all signatories to the Genocide Convention, a case like this where neither side is a direct party to a conflict is unusual. Its represenatives told the court that Nicaragua had not taken the proper steps before filing the legal challenge and arguing much of the case falls out of the ICJ's jurisdiction.

"Germany respectfully requests the court to reject Nicaragua's claims," Julia Monar, legal adviser to the German Foreign Ministry, told the judges.

"All German weapons exports to Israel and other countries are subject to strict review procedures that are more stringent than international regulations," Monar also told the court, a reference to Germany's intentionally restrictive weapons export policies adopted after World War II.

In mid-May this year, Germany's Bundestag parliament published information saying that between November 2025 — shortly after the truce was brokered — and March this year, exports worth around €167 million (roughly $194 million) were approved.

What's likely to happen next?

Nicaragua's case is based on the South African lawsuit at the ICJ accusing Israel of genocidal acts in Gaza.

In a preliminary hearing — the findings of which Israel rejected — the court found it plausible that Israel could have committed genocidal acts in Gaza and called for a full hearing. That process will take years, with court sessions not expected until 2029.

A full hearing in Nicaragua's case against Germany, should the ICJ choose to pursue one, could well rely on a resolution in the broader genocide allegations against Israel.

More immediately, Nicaragua is expected to lay out its arguments in The Hague on Tuesday.

A decision on Germany's bid to shelve the case entirely is tentatively expected some time this year.

The ICJ is the top UN court dealing with disputes between states and alleged violations of various international treaties. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
entries.summary: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the Saxony-Anhalt state election but without an absolute majority in parliament. Other European nations were wrestling with the impact of the results. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Germany

Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory

Published September 6, 2026last updated September 7, 2026

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the Saxony-Anhalt state election but without an absolute majority in parliament. Other European nations were wrestling with the impact of the results. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
  • AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
  • Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
  • Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
  • Merz says CDU shaken 'to its very foundations' by AfD win
  • The European press calling the results an 'unsettling new page in German history'

Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.

Skip next section Under fire from Merz for campaign comments, CDU's Sepp Müller seeks Saxony-Anhalt leadership

Under fire from Merz for campaign comments, CDU's Sepp Müller seeks Saxony-Anhalt leadership

The Bundestag lawmaker Sepp Müller has told a meeting of senior state party officials in Saxony-Anhalt that he wants to take over as party leader in the state. 

State Premier Sven Schulze resigned as CDU state chairman in the aftermath of Sunday's disastrous showing at the polls, when the party lost almost 20% of the vote share compared to 2021, falling to 17.2% and a distant second to the AfD.

"I am standing as a candidate for state chairman," Müller said after Monday's meeting in Magdeburg.

But the 37-year-old's candidacy comes as he faces stern criticism from federal CDU leaders, not least Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

This is because of his comments in the run-up to the vote. Müller appeared on a Politico's "Berlin Playbook" podcast and said that if the polls were anything to go by, then the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund had a mandate to try to form a government. He made comparable comments elsewhere during the week.

Some might argue that Müller was stating the obvious, and describing the situation that later came to pass, but Merz and other CDU leaders called it an inexplicable broadside undermining the closing phases of the party's own election campaign.

Merz told CDU leaders in a national meeting on Monday that "none of us understood" why "a deputy leader of our parliamentary group would stab the party's own top candidate in the back in such a way as repeatedly happened from three days before the vote until yesterday."

Party group chairman Thorsten Frei was also critical of Müller, saying that while almost any thought experiments and disagreements were permissible in the right circumstances, such public musings days before a crucial vote were "problematic in the highest degree."

In any case, Frei said, Sven Schulze and the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt "did not perceive it as campaign support," concluding, "therefore it would have been better left unsaid."

Skip next section EU's Kallas warn of Russian hybrid threat and parties that 'ignore this'

EU's Kallas warn of Russian hybrid threat and parties that 'ignore this'

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas was in Vilnius in Lithuania on Monday and was asked during the press conference what the AfD's election performance could mean for the EU.

Although she did not call out the party or its politicians by name, she put developments in the context of Russian hybrid attacks and threats, including the alleged attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"We have seen the attack in Leipzig and the acts of sabotage and the threat in Europe is increasing considerably," Kallas said. "At the same time parties are gaining influence that ignore this threat and say that we should not do anything about it because it does not concern us."

Kallas had also discussed Leipzig and hybrid threats prior to the question-and-answer session.

During her press conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius, she said she worried that Europe might "one day realize that we did not do enough" to protect itself from these threats.

However, Kallas stressed that it was ultimately up to the German people to make its own democratic choices.

Sinkevicius — the leader of one of the EU members that was once part of the Soviet Union, as the Estonian former PM Kallas once was — also referred to the result as "concerning." 

Skip next section In pictures — Protest at Brandenburg Gate in Berlin after AfD win

In pictures — Protest at Brandenburg Gate in Berlin after AfD win

Police in Berlin said that more than 2,500 people gathered for a demonstration organized by the Campact and Fridays for Future activist groups on Monday, following the AfD's unprecedented state election performance in Saxony-Anhalt.

Leading politicians from the Greens and the Left Party also attended the event, not long before elections in the city state of Berlin.

People carried a variety of placards and banners, often either criticizing the AfD or in some cases even calling for attempts to ban the party. They chanted slogans like "everyone united against fascism."

The German capital is in campaign mode itself at present with politicians of all stripes campaigning at or near the Brandenburg Gate.

The September 20 election is likely to be a much more close-fought event, but even in the notoriously left-leaning German capital the AfD is hoping to secure its best ever vote share — it's essentially in a five-way fight to emerge as the largest single party.

Not far west, a similar but smaller demonstration also took place at the Alter Markt ("Old Marketplace") central square in Potsdam on Monday evening.

Skip next section CDU's Jürgen Hardt: Result also shows lack of confidence in federal government and Merz

CDU's Jürgen Hardt: Result also shows lack of confidence in federal government and Merz

The CDU's Jürgen Hardt, a senior party figure on foreign policy and lawmaker in the Bundestag in Berlin, spoke with DW's Chief Political Editor Michaela Küfner about the implications of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.

He said the federal government and party leadership should be under no illusions that the result was "not only due to the internal questions of Saxony-Anhalt," but also due to a lack of confidence with the federal government and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

"To be frank, it should that our concept to minimize the results of the AfD did not work out yet," he said. "We tried to counter AfD support by doing good politics, expecially in the field of migration," Hardt said, pointing to the sharp reduction in asylum applications over the last two years and a gradual return towards economic growth.

"But this is not what voters in Saxony-Anhalt are interested in," he surmised. "They probably want to show 'we are [not] confident in the chancellor and his policy,' and this message needs to be heard by us."

Asked what should be done, Hardt effectively said more of the same — but better and with better communication and salesmanship. He said he hoped the results would not derail or complicate either domestic reforms programs or foreign policy issues like support for Ukraine. 

Hardt 'expects' that AfD's Siegmund will lead the state government

Hardt also said, even as the AfD casts doubt on this in the aftermath of the vote, that he believed the party would ultimately lead the state government — with or without a majority, saying he "expected" Ulrich Siegmund to become state premier.

"He has 39 votes, he needs three extra votes and I am sure that from BSW he will get those votes in the end," Hardt said, referring to the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or BSW.

But even if not, Hardt said that with "a relative majority of 39 seats" Siegmund and the AfD would still have more parliamentary control than the CDU, Social Democrats and Greens combining their 32 seats.

"I'm sure that Siegmund will do that. He's now talking about new elections — something like that — but at the end of the day, he wants to become state premier, he has to deliver, and he cannot hide away," Hardt said.

Even if this came to pass, Hardt said a state government cannot have "much influence" on foreign security issues in German politics, "and therefore I am not in panic" about what it might mean for Germany or its allies.

He did however warn about the AfD's stance on Ukraine and Russia, calling the party a Russian "trojan horse" in German politics that he said advocated policies which would lead to Germany "depending on Russia" and having "to follow the directives of this dictator" Vladimir Putin.

Skip next section German Chancellor Merz rules out cooperation with AfD but says CDU 'shaken to foundation'

German Chancellor Merz rules out cooperation with AfD but says CDU 'shaken to foundation'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday doubled down on his refusal to work with the far-right populist AfD while at the same time admitting that Sunday's election drubbing had shaken his own conservative CDU "to its very foundations."

AfD has siphoned off CDU voters and pushed Merz's conservatives farther to the right, now it is hoping to win over some of its lawmakers in the state of Saxony-Anhalt in order to form a ruling coalition as it fell just short of winning an outright majority.

Merz said during a press conference on Monday in Berlin after the election: "This shakes our party to its very foundations. We cannot simply carry on as before, nor can I, nor can the federal government."

"We have a strong constitution; we have all the tools to defend the constitution against a right-wing extremist state government," added the deeply unpopular Merz, "but our party system is ​undergoing a tectonic shift."

Both AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla and top candidate Ulrich Siegmund have called on CDU lawmakers in the state to drop the "deeply undemocratic" firewall and work toward creating a "center-right conservative majority" in Saxony-Anhalt — with Chrupalla saying, "Partisan games really ought to be a thing of ‌the past."

Skip next section Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD

Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD

Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."

Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.

Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."

For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.

It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.

Skip next section AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'

AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'

Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.

He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.

Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.

Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.

She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.

This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.

Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."

Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.

Skip next section AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference

AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference

In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state. 

Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.

Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.

Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.

Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.

After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.

After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.

Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.

Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."

Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.

"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."

Skip next section What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?

What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?

Skip next section Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'

Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'

Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."

Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"

After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era. 

Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."

Skip next section Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now

Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now

Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.

After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.

Skip next section Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory

Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory

The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.

The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.

Skip next section International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'

International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'

Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.

New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.

In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.

Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."

And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."

Skip next section Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt

Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt

Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory. 

"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.



Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."

"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.

Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.

Skip next section Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'

Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'

Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.

"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.

Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.

She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."

The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.

"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.

entries.title: Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?
entries.summary: Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without the absolute majority?
entries.content:
Germany

Can the AfD form a government in Saxony-Anhalt?

September 7, 2026

Following its record election success, the far-right Alternative for Germany aims to form a government. What options does it have without the absolute majority?

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in the eastern German state quite difficult.

The day after the election, party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla held a press conference in Berlin. They were joined by the winner of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. 

Even though the AfD narrowly missed its main election goal of being able to govern alone with an absolute majority, it is now more confident than ever before. The party leaders made clear that they are thinking not just about Saxony-Anhalt, but about all of Germany, and are convinced they will govern the whole country in the not-so-distant future.

"The CDU/CSU will never again be able to win a federal election. That is a fact," party co-chair Weidel announced in reference to the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union, which leads the national government. 

"My stated goal is to widen the gap as quickly as possible and reach at least 40% in the next federal election," said Weidel, who wants to become Germany's next chancellor.

Cooperation: Yes — but with whom?

But how exactly to proceed in Saxony-Anhalt? Who does the AfD want to bring on board to form an AfD state government?

Much remains unclear even the day after the election. AfD lead candidate Siegmund repeatedly emphasized on Monday: "We extend a hand to every political actor in Saxony-Anhalt." However, he always adds that his willingness to compromise is very limited.

"We will remain true to ourselves. We will not compromise our principles," Siegmund said.

The AfD leaders say they want to form a stable government. This would rule out a minority government that would have to seek majorities in the state parliament on a vote-by-vote basis.

On election night, Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me."

Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.

The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: It has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an interview with public broadcaster ARD that these issues are non-negotiable.

Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.

On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."

Could the BSW help the AfD form a government?

The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which cleared the 5% threshold for representation in parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

This article has been translated from German. It was published on September 6 and updated the following day to reflect news developments.

entries.title: Russia announces it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg
entries.summary: The tit-for-tat reaction comes after Germany said it is shutting down Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural center in Berlin.
entries.content:
Germany

Russia says it is closing German consulate in St. Petersburg

September 7, 2026

The tit-for-tat reaction comes after Germany said it is shutting down Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural center in Berlin.

The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.  

The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 at the latest, according to the Foreign Ministry.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.

Russia also earlier ordered the closure of all Goethe-Institut branches on Russian territory, with Goethe-Institut staff having to leave the country by September 13.

Goethe-Institut is a center that promotes German language and culture. Goethe-Institut is largely financed by the German government.

Germany, Russia trade barbs over Leipzig drone attack

The moves are a direct response to Germany's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin, a decision Russia labeled "unfriendly."

Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport.

The EU, too, said the incident had all the signs of "state sponsored terrorism."

The Leipzig airport is an important international freight hub, also used for providing support to Ukraine.

Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected Germany's allegations, calling them "the beginning of a real war."

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: War criminal Ratko Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade, Serbia
entries.summary: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb commander convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, has been buried in Belgrade. The funeral, broadcast live on TV, comes just days before President Vucic is expected to call an election.
entries.content:
Serbia

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade

September 7, 2026

Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb commander convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, has been buried in Belgrade. The funeral, broadcast live on TV, comes just days before President Vucic is expected to call an election.

Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.

Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.

Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.

President Vucic not in attendance

President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.

Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.

Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.

"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.

The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.

Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.

An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."

Politically tricky time for Vucic

For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.

He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.

For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.

Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.

Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina

According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.

"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."

Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.

Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.

"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."

Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.

Students have a different focus

In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.

Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.

In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.

The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.

The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.

Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.

The power of media control

Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.

The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.

In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."

Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.

Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
entries.summary: A visibly shaken but also determined Friedrich Merz spoke in Berlin about the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt and the CDU's bitter defeat. He insisted on sticking to his reforms.
entries.content:
Germany

Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'

September 7, 2026

A visibly shaken but also determined Friedrich Merz spoke in Berlin about the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt and the CDU's bitter defeat. He insisted on sticking to his reforms.

There are situations in which politicians who have little left to say to each other still appear together before the press. This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.

He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."

This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.

No regard for the rule of law?

Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.

But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.

In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."

Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.

Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."

Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?

Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.

As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.

And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?

If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.

Merz defends his controversial reforms

However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.

On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.

AfD displays confidence

Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.

"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."

For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.

Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."

But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
entries.summary: Europe just opened a carbon capture and storage plant billed as the continent's largest. But global climate scenarios call for far more capacity than exists anywhere on Earth.
entries.content:
September 7, 2026

Europe just opened a carbon capture and storage plant billed as the continent's largest. But global climate scenarios call for far more capacity than exists anywhere on Earth.

For years there has been talk of capturing and storing the carbon dioxide generated by burning fossil fuels as one way to keep the planet from overheating. In fact, the United Nations' climate science body envisions somewhere between 350 to 1,200 gigatons of CO2 storage within the century to avoid the worst effects of climate change. 

But is it really happening? Yes and no.

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is an effort to trap CO2 at what's called a point source. This might be a smokestack or at an ammonia factory — in other words, a single, concentrated spot where the planet-heating greenhouse gas is emitted.  

After being captured, it is compressed and transported, usually using pipelines or trains, before being stored geologically — in aquifers or old oil reservoirs, for example.

CCS is related to, but distinct from, carbon dioxide removal (CDR), which involves pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere after it's already been emitted. That CO2 is often stored similarly to CCS, but uses very different technologies for capturing. 

"Given the legacy of emissions in the atmosphere, given where we are in terms of emissions reductions, we're going to need these approaches," said Wil Burns, co-director of the Institute for Carbon Removal Law & Policy at American University.

"We just have to figure out how to use them thoughtfully and still keep our eye on the prize of decarbonizing."

The technology works, but scaling is another matter

The feasibility of CCS and CDR is a subject of much debate among scientists and climate campaigners.

Advocates for scaling up the technology as a key pillar of decarbonization say the main hurdle is getting more plants built, which would require government subsidies and policy intervention.

Without governments putting a price on carbon or offering tax credits, experts say it's hard to imagine investors shelling out for these expensive commercial projects. Renewable energy, by contrast, has become so cheap over time that it's often commercially viable on its own.

"It's ready to go, technologically. We know how to do this process," said Susan Hovorka, a geoscientist at the University of Texas-Austin, researching CCS since 1998.

How CCS began

CCS traces its roots back to the 1960s, when oil companies began piping natural CO2 into oil fields for enhanced oil recovery — that's where captured CO2 is injected into old oil fields to help push more oil out of the ground. It wasn't until 1996 that the first large-scale CCS project designed to reduce emissions went online in Norway. 

Progress since then has been slowly ramping up. In 2020, there were 26 operational commercial CCS facilities around the world. As of last summer, the number has nearly tripled.

But others say the technology remains in its infancy, and our real-world capabilities lag far behind our technical knowhow.

"What is not well-established and basically doesn't exist at scale is the commercial experience doing this," said Danny Cullenward, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. "And proving that it works; that it's easy, that it's cost-effective, that it can be deployed at large scale, that it works in lots of different places."

Researchers from the University of Texas-Austin recently revealedthat though small-scale pilot projects have been successful in injecting CO2 into the ground, many of the world's large-scale CCS initiatives are pumping far less into storage sites than promised. 

And they are not unlimited. While previous estimates put the Earth's CO2 storage capacity somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 gigatons, a new study foundthe number is just about 1,460 gigatons, meaning most CCS-reliant climate scenarios would breach the planetary limit for storage over the next 250 years. 

Climate models bet heavy on new technology

Starting this week, the European fertilizer giant Yara will open what it calls Europe's largest carbon capture project. It will harvest excess CO2 at its factory in Sluiskil Netherlands, liquefy it, and ship it to Norway's Atlantic coast to be stored in an underground rock formation, some 2,600 meters below the seabed.

That plant will only be able to capture 800,000 metric tons of CO2 annually. To meet that 350 gigaton threshold — the lower end of the UN's climate scenarios used to inform climate policy — would require about 5,800 more Yara-size plants to open tomorrow.

The International Energy Agency, another intergovernmental body that models climate data, projected7.6 gigatons of carbon will be captured every year by 2050, with almost all of it stored. Right now, the world's 77 operating plants are capable of capturing 64 million tons annually. That output would need to be multiplied by 119 over the next quarter-century to reach the IEA number. 

"The scale of what's being called for in those scenarios is astronomically beyond any real activity that exists today," Cullenward said.

He says climate models tend to underestimate renewables and lean too hard on "gee-whiz" technologies.

That's because models basically have three ways to hit an ambitious climate target: add more renewables, use less energy, or bet on some new technology that solves the problem without forcing society to change much.

"If you tell a model to solve an impossible problem, it's like pouring water down a flight of stairs — it's going to find the fastest way to get to the bottom," Cullenward said.

A license to keep drilling?

One of the most contentious arguments about CCS is whether it represents a legitimate decarbonization solution or is a tactic from oil and gas companies to justify and prolong more fossil fuel extraction.

In 2023, about 80% of the world's CCS capacity was used for enhanced oil recovery, according to research and advocacy group, Oil Change International — ultimately increasing emissions and defeating CCS's climate benefit.  

Some researchers also argue that CCS poses a moral hazard, or a situation where having a form of protection allows for more risk-taking.

On the other hand, advocates for the technology often talk of reserving CCS for what's called "hard-to-abate" industries, like cement.

"I don't think we're going to get to five or 10 or 20 gigatons a year of carbon removal," Cullenward said. "But we may need to get as much as we can and to me that's a reason to be more engaged rather than less engaged."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
entries.summary: Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether simply creating more provinces is the solution.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?

September 7, 2026

Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether simply creating more provinces is the solution.

A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.  

Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative "reset" in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.

Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.

Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.

Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.

There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.

More provinces, better governance?

Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.

"Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people," Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.

Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan's four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.

Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.

Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan's growing population.

But there is disagreement over the solution.

"Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level," Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.

He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.

Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.

Altering the political balance

"Pakistan's history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services," Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.

The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.

Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.

New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.

Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.

The political resistance has already begun, with Sindh's provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.

A risky strategy?

Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.

"Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge," he said.

"Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus," he added.

The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.

Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.

He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.

"We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services," Ismail said.

Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.

"In Pakistan's case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions," he said.

For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.

It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions.
